name: Rudolf Nureyev
milestone_by_age_26: Upon graduating from the Vaganova Academy in 1958 at age 20, Nureyev became a principal soloist with the Kirov Ballet, one of the world's premier companies, and by 23 he defected to the West and became an international ballet sensation.
early_history_summary: Nureyev began ballet training at age 11 in Ufa and entered the Vaganova Academy of Russian Ballet in Leningrad at age 17 in 1955, where he studied under Alexander Pushkin. Upon graduation in 1958, he immediately became a principal soloist with the Kirov Ballet, dancing 15 roles in three years. In June 1961 at age 23, he defected at Le Bourget Airport in Paris and became an international star, joining the Royal Ballet with Margot Fonteyn by early 1962.
family_context_summary: Born to a Tatar Muslim family in the Soviet Union; his father was a Red Army political commissar. The family was poor and Nureyev's early life was disrupted by wartime displacement. He was the only son with three older sisters.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. No evidence of family connections to ballet or the arts.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Vaganova Academy,Kirov Ballet,Alexander Pushkin mentor,Leningrad ballet ecosystem,late start physical talent
evidence_summary: Nureyev began ballet at 11 in Ufa and entered the elite Vaganova Academy in Leningrad at 17, studying under renowned ballet master Alexander Pushkin, who allowed him to live with his family. Upon graduation in 1958 at age 20, he immediately became a principal soloist with the Kirov Ballet, dancing 15 roles in three years and becoming one of the Soviet Union's best-known dancers. His 1961 defection at age 23 made him an international sensation, leading to his partnership with Margot Fonteyn at the Royal Ballet. His primary advantages were the elite Vaganova/Kirov pipeline and Pushkin's sustained mentorship; his family provided no financial or domain advantage, and his late start and Soviet-era constraints created significant adversity.

name: Anne Frank
milestone_by_age_26: Anne Frank died in Bergen-Belsen in 1945 at age 15. Her diary was published posthumously in 1947 by her father Otto Frank. No material, independently verifiable milestone occurred during her lifetime by age 26; recognition came entirely posthumously.
early_history_summary: Frank received a diary for her 13th birthday in June 1942 and wrote entries while hiding with her family in the Secret Annex in Amsterdam from July 1942 to August 1944. She was arrested on August 4, 1944 and died in Bergen-Belsen concentration camp in early 1945. Her father Otto Frank edited and published the diary as 'Het Achterhuis' in June 1947.
family_context_summary: Born to a Jewish family in Frankfurt, Germany. Her father Otto Frank was a banker and businessman. The family fled Nazi Germany to Amsterdam in 1933. The diary was written while the family was in hiding from Nazi persecution.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father Otto Frank was a businessman and banker, providing a middle-class upbringing. No evidence of literary or publishing family background.
evidence_summary: Anne Frank died at age 15 in 1945 at Bergen-Belsen concentration camp. Her diary, written between ages 13 and 15, was published posthumously in 1947 by her father Otto Frank. While the diary became one of the most widely read books in history, no material milestone occurred during her lifetime by age 26. All recognition and publication came posthumously, making her ineligible under the milestone-by-26 criterion.

name: Norman Foster, Baron Foster of Thames Bank
milestone_by_age_26: Foster graduated from the University of Manchester School of Architecture in 1961 at age 26 and won a Henry Fellowship to Yale, but his architectural practice (Team 4, formed 1963) and major built works came later. No material creative milestone by 26; the fellowship was a credential, not a built work or design achievement.
early_history_summary: Foster left school at 16, worked in Manchester's City Treasurer's office, and did National Service in the RAF. He entered the University of Manchester School of Architecture at age 21 in 1956, working odd jobs to pay his way. He graduated in 1961 and won a Henry Fellowship to Yale, where he earned his Master of Architecture in 1962 and met Richard Rogers. Their firm Team 4 was formed in 1963.
family_context_summary: Born to a working-class family in Reddish, Stockport. His father was a machine painter at Metropolitan-Vickers works and his mother worked in a local bakery. The family lived in poverty in Levenshulme, Manchester. Foster was an only child.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. Father worked in a factory; no evidence of architectural or design family background.
evidence_summary: Foster graduated from Manchester's architecture school in 1961 at age 26 and won a Henry Fellowship to Yale. While this was a notable credential, his first architectural practice (Team 4) was not formed until 1963 and his major built works came even later. The fellowship represents academic achievement rather than a material creative milestone. He came from a working-class family in Manchester with no architectural background, working multiple jobs to fund his education.

name: Jaggi Vasudev
milestone_by_age_26: At age 25 (1982), Vasudev shut down his businesses after a spiritual experience; he taught his first yoga class in 1983 at age 26 with seven participants. The Isha Foundation was established in 1992 at age 35. No material, independently verifiable milestone by 26.
early_history_summary: Vasudev graduated from the University of Mysore with a degree in English literature, then started a poultry farm and a construction company (Buildaids). At age 25 on September 23, 1982, he had a spiritual experience on Chamundi Hill and left his businesses. After about a year of travel and meditation, he taught his first yoga class in Mysore in 1983 with seven participants. The Isha Foundation was established near Coimbatore in 1992.
family_context_summary: Born into a Telugu family in Mysore. His father was an ophthalmologist at the Mysuru Railway Hospital and his mother was a homemaker. He was the youngest of five children. The family was middle-class.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a physician (ophthalmologist). No evidence of spiritual or yoga-specific family background. Family moved frequently due to father's job transfers.
evidence_summary: By age 26 (1983), Vasudev had just begun teaching yoga with a first class of seven participants in Mysore, having shut down his poultry and construction businesses after a spiritual experience at age 25. The Isha Foundation, his major institutional milestone, was not established until 1992 when he was 35. No material, independently verifiable milestone occurred by age 26; his first yoga class was a small, informal event with no broader recognition.

name: Debbie Reynolds
milestone_by_age_26: At age 19, Reynolds starred as Kathy Selden in Singin' in the Rain (1952), one of the greatest movie musicals ever made, launching her as a major Hollywood star; by 26 she had multiple hit films and a number-one Billboard single.
early_history_summary: Reynolds won the Miss Burbank beauty contest at age 16 in 1948, leading to a contract with Warner Bros. She moved to MGM and appeared in several film musicals. Her breakout role came at 19 when she starred opposite Gene Kelly in Singin' in the Rain (1952), despite having no formal dance training. Kelly taught her to dance during production. She followed with hit films including The Affairs of Dobie Gillis (1953), Susan Slept Here (1954), and Tammy and the Bachelor (1957), whose title song topped the Billboard charts.
family_context_summary: Born in El Paso, Texas to a working-class family. Her father was a carpenter for the Southern Pacific Railroad and her mother took in laundry. The family lived in a shack and moved to Burbank, California in 1939. She was raised in a strict Nazarene church environment.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. No evidence of family connections to entertainment or the arts.
primary_early_advantage_tags: MGM studio system,Gene Kelly mentor,Golden Age Hollywood musicals,beauty contest discovery,working-class drive
evidence_summary: Reynolds was discovered at 16 via the Miss Burbank contest in 1948, leading to a Warner Bros. contract and then MGM. At 19, with no formal dance training, she starred opposite Gene Kelly in Singin' in the Rain (1952), which Kelly taught her to dance for during production. The film made her a major star. Her primary advantage was the MGM studio system, the premier talent pipeline of Golden Age Hollywood, combined with Kelly's mentorship. Her working-class background provided no financial or family-domain advantage, but poverty drove her ambition. By 26 she had multiple hit films and a number-one Billboard single with 'Tammy' (1957).

name: Grace Kelly
milestone_by_age_26: At age 25, Kelly won the Academy Award for Best Actress for The Country Girl (1954) and the New York Film Critics Circle Award, having already starred in High Noon, Mogambo, Rear Window, and Dial M for Murder by that age.
early_history_summary: Kelly was born into a prominent Philadelphia family and attended the American Academy of Dramatic Arts in New York, graduating in 1949. She made her Broadway debut in The Father that year and appeared in nearly sixty live television programs. Her film debut came in Fourteen Hours (1951), followed by her breakthrough in High Noon (1952). By 1953, Mogambo earned her a Golden Globe and Oscar nomination. In 1954 alone, she starred in Dial M for Murder, Rear Window, The Country Girl (winning the Oscar), and The Bridges at Toko-Ri. She retired from acting at 26 to marry Prince Rainier III of Monaco.
family_context_summary: Born into an affluent and influential Philadelphia Catholic family. Her father John B. Kelly Sr. was a three-time Olympic gold medalist in sculling and a wealthy brickwork contractor. Her uncle George Kelly was a Pulitzer Prize-winning dramatist, and uncle Walter Kelly was a vaudeville star. Her mother Margaret Majer was the first woman to coach women's athletics at the University of Pennsylvania.
primary_early_advantage_tags: American Academy of Dramatic Arts,uncle George Kelly mentor,wealthy family,Hitchcock mentor,Golden Age Hollywood,Philadelphia social prominence
evidence_summary: Kelly was born into a wealthy Philadelphia family with strong artistic connections: her uncle George Kelly was a Pulitzer Prize-winning dramatist who helped her gain admission to the American Academy of Dramatic Arts and mentored her throughout her early career. She graduated from AADA in 1949, made her Broadway debut, and appeared in nearly sixty live TV programs before her film debut in 1951. By 25, she had won the Academy Award for Best Actress for The Country Girl (1954), starred in Hitchcock's Rear Window and Dial M for Murder, and been nominated for Mogambo. Her advantages were substantial: family wealth and prominence, uncle's mentorship and industry connections, elite training at AADA, and access to top Hollywood directors including Hitchcock, Ford, and Zinnemann. She retired from acting at 26 to become Princess of Monaco.

name: Yul Brynner
milestone_by_age_26: By age 26 (1946), Brynner had made his Broadway debut in Lute Song but in a supporting role; his defining breakthrough came with The King and I on Broadway in 1951 at age 31. No material milestone by 26.
early_history_summary: Brynner was born in Vladivostok and moved to Paris as a teenager, where he played guitar in nightclubs and worked as a trapeze artist. He moved to the U.S. in 1941 to study with Michael Chekhov's theatrical troupe. He made his Broadway debut in Lute Song (1946) and worked in early television as a director at CBS. His film debut was Port of New York (1949). His career-defining role as the King of Siam in The King and I came in 1951.
family_context_summary: Born in Vladivostok to a father of Swiss-German and Russian descent who was an engineer and inventor, and a Russian mother. His father abandoned the family, and his mother took him and his sister to Harbin, China, then to Paris. He attended the exclusive Lycée Moncelle but dropped out.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was an engineer and inventor of Swiss-German and Russian descent. No evidence of performing arts family background. Family was separated when Brynner was young.
evidence_summary: By age 26 (1946), Brynner had made his Broadway debut in Lute Song alongside Mary Martin, but this was a supporting role and did not constitute a material milestone. Before that, he had been a nightclub guitarist, trapeze artist, and CBS television director. His career-defining breakthrough came at 31 with The King and I (1951), which won him a Tony Award and launched his international fame. No material, independently verifiable milestone occurred by age 26.

name: Erwin Neher
milestone_by_age_26: Neher completed his PhD in physics at TU Munich in 1970 at age 26, but his Nobel-winning patch clamp technique was developed with Bert Sakmann in the mid-1970s. The PhD was a credential, not a material scientific milestone.
early_history_summary: Neher studied physics at the Technical University of Munich, earned a Fulbright Scholarship to the University of Wisconsin-Madison in 1966 where he received an MSc in 1967, then returned to Munich for PhD studies at the Max Planck Institute for Psychiatry under H.D. Lux. His doctoral thesis on nerve cell membranes was completed in 1970. He moved to the Max Planck Institute for Biophysical Chemistry in Göttingen in 1972 and began the collaboration with Bert Sakmann that led to the patch clamp technique, published in 1981 and recognized with the 1991 Nobel Prize.
family_context_summary: Born in Landsberg, Germany. Attended a Catholic Gymnasium (Maristenkolleg) in Mindelheim. No evidence of family financial privilege or scientific family background in reviewed sources.

While this was a solid academic credential, his Nobel-winning patch clamp technique was developed with Bert Sakmann in the mid-to-late 1970s at the Max Planck Institute in Göttingen, with the landmark publication appearing in 1981. No material, independently verifiable scientific milestone occurred by age 26; the PhD was an expected academic step rather than a breakthrough achievement.

name: Michel Mayor
milestone_by_age_26: By age 26 (1968), Mayor had earned a Master's in Physics (1966) and a Certificat d'Astronomie from Geneva (1968), but was still a PhD student. His Nobel-winning discovery of 51 Pegasi b came in 1995 at age 53. No material milestone by 26.
early_history_summary: Mayor studied theoretical physics at the University of Lausanne, earning a Master's in 1966. He then moved to astrophysics at the University of Geneva, obtaining a Certificat d'Astronomie et d'Astrophysique in 1968. His PhD on stellar kinematics and galactic spiral structure was completed in 1971 at age 29. He spent his career at the University of Geneva, becoming a professor in 1988. His discovery of the first exoplanet orbiting a sun-like star, 51 Pegasi b, was made with Didier Queloz in 1995, earning the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physics.

name: Psy
milestone_by_age_26: Psy released his debut album in January 2001 at age 23, selling 124,000 copies domestically, but his global breakthrough came with Gangnam Style in 2012 at age 35. The debut album was a domestic niche success, not a material milestone on the required scale.
early_history_summary: Psy attended Boston University and then Berklee College of Music but dropped out of both without a degree. He returned to South Korea and debuted with the album 'Psy from the Psycho World!' in January 2001, which sold 124,000 copies and was the 75th best-selling album of the year in South Korea. He was fined for the album's 'inappropriate content' and gained the nickname 'The Bizarre Singer.' He released several more domestic albums through the 2000s but remained a domestic artist until Gangnam Style (2012) became a global viral phenomenon.
family_context_summary: Born Park Jae-sang in South Korea. Attended Boston University and Berklee College of Music but dropped out of both. Family financial background not clearly documented in reviewed sources, though attendance at U.S. universities suggests some means.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. No evidence of family music industry connections.
evidence_summary: Psy released his debut album at age 23 in January 2001, selling approximately 124,000 copies in South Korea and ranking 75th for the year. While this was a domestic niche success that stirred the Korean pop scene, it was not a material milestone on the scale required. His global fame arrived 11 years later with Gangnam Style (2012), which became the first YouTube video to reach 1 billion views. By age 26 (2003), he had released two more domestic albums but had not achieved a material, independently verifiable milestone of lasting significance.

name: Sigourney Weaver
milestone_by_age_26: By age 26 (1975), Weaver had graduated from Yale Drama School (1974) and was performing in off-Broadway shows. Her breakthrough role as Ellen Ripley in Alien came in 1979 at age 30. No material milestone by 26.
early_history_summary: Weaver attended Stanford University, graduating with a BA in English in 1972, then studied drama at Yale School of Drama, completing her MFA in 1974. Her teachers at Yale told her she lacked talent, damaging her confidence. After graduation, she worked in off-Broadway productions and had a small role in the soap opera Somerset. Her first film appearance was a minor role in Annie Hall (1977). Her breakthrough came when Ridley Scott cast her as Ellen Ripley in Alien (1979).
family_context_summary: Born into New York City's media elite. Her father Sylvester 'Pat' Weaver was president of NBC in the 1950s. Her mother Elizabeth Inglis was an English actress who appeared in Alfred Hitchcock's The 39 Steps (1935) and The Letter (1940). She attended private schools including the Ethel Walker School in Connecticut.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was president of NBC, a major television network. Mother was a professional actress. Family was deeply embedded in the entertainment industry, though Weaver said her parents called the business 'the racket' and were cautious about it.
evidence_summary: By age 26 (1975), Weaver had completed her MFA at Yale Drama School in 1974 and was performing in off-Broadway shows with no major roles. Her teachers at Yale had told her she lacked acting talent. Her first film appearance was a minor role in Annie Hall (1977) at age 28, and her breakthrough as Ellen Ripley in Alien came in 1979 at age 30. Despite being born into a prominent entertainment family (father was NBC president, mother was a professional actress), no material, independently verifiable milestone occurred by age 26.
